report.tagline: A credit-card-sized AI voice recorder that turns your meetings, calls and lectures into transcripts and summaries.
report.simpleSummary: Plaud sells a small recorder, about as thin as a few credit cards, that sticks to the back of your phone or clips on your shirt. You press one button and it records a meeting, a phone call or a doctor visit. The Plaud app then writes out every word and gives you a short summary and to-do list. You get some free minutes each month, and you pay a yearly fee if you need more.

overview.whatItDoes: Plaud makes AI voice recorders: Plaud Note and Note Pro (card shaped, sits on the back of a phone) and NotePin (a small wearable pin). The device records audio, and the Plaud app sends it to AI models that transcribe it, label who spoke, and write summaries. Plaud earns money twice: once when you buy the device and again every year if you subscribe for more minutes and features.
howItWorks: You buy a device for roughly $159 to $179 on Amazon, Best Buy, Costco or plaud.ai.
You press one button to start recording. For phone calls, Note uses a vibration sensor to capture both sides of the call through the phone body.
Audio syncs to the Plaud app over Bluetooth or Wi-Fi.
The app transcribes the recording in over 100 languages and labels speakers.
You pick a summary template (meeting notes, sales call, doctor visit, lecture) and get a summary, mind map and action items.
Ask Plaud lets you ask questions across all your past recordings, like 'What did the client say about pricing last week?'
overview.valueProposition: You stop taking notes and start listening. Unlike a phone app or a Zoom bot, Plaud works in person and on calls, with one button and no setup.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Thin card recorder that attaches to a phone with a magnet. Note Pro adds a small screen and longer range.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: The hardware is the front door. It gets Plaud into people's hands through retail, where software apps cannot be sold.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: A wearable pin you clip on a shirt or wear on the wrist.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: Captures conversations on the move, which widens daily use beyond desk meetings.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Turns audio into text in over 100 languages and marks who said what.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: The basic job users pay for. Accuracy decides whether they trust it.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Ready formats for sales calls, medical visits, lectures and more.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: Makes the output useful for a specific job, which is what justifies paying for Pro.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Chat with your recordings to find facts or draft follow-ups.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: The more you record, the more useful it becomes, which raises switching costs.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Free Starter plan with 300 minutes a month, Pro at $99.99 a year, Unlimited at $239.99 a year.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: This is the recurring revenue that turns a one-time gadget sale into a lasting business.

businessModel.summary: Plaud makes money from two things: selling the recorder, and yearly subscriptions for more AI minutes and features. The device is profitable on its own and also brings in subscribers.

revenueStreams.detail: Note, Note Pro and NotePin sold for roughly $159 to $179 through its site, Amazon, Best Buy and Costco. Most of the estimated $250 million 2025 revenue.
Pro at $99.99 a year and Unlimited at $239.99 a year. Passed $100 million ARR in June 2026.
Extra transcription minutes, for example 3,000 minutes for $59.99.
Cases, wrist straps, clips and retail bundles that include months of Pro.

businessModel.pricing: Device about $159 to $179. Starter plan free with 300 minutes a month. Pro $99.99 a year. Unlimited $239.99 a year.
costDrivers: AI model costs for transcription and summaries, which grow with every minute recorded
Making the device (parts, factory, packaging) and shipping
Retail margins paid to Amazon, Best Buy and Costco
Marketing through influencers, YouTube reviewers and ads
businessModel.unitEconomics: Rough estimate for one customer: Plaud sells a $159 device. After making it, shipping it and paying the retailer, it may keep about $50 to $70. If that buyer then pays $99.99 a year for Pro, and records about 1,200 minutes a month, AI costs might be $2 to $5 a month, so Plaud keeps roughly $40 to $75 a year from the plan. Unlimited users who record all day cost much more to serve, so their margin is thinner. The key is that the device sale already pays back the cost of getting the customer, so every subscription year is mostly extra profit.

whatBringsUsersBack: Every meeting is a new reason to press the button

growth.moat: Plaud's lead is in distribution and habit. It has 2 million devices in pockets and shelf space at big retailers. Phone makers and meeting apps can copy the software, but a dedicated device that works in person and on calls, with years of a user's recordings inside it, is harder to replace. The moat is not deep: AI models are available to anyone, so Plaud must keep winning on hardware design and workflow features.

competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Plaud does not need a laptop or a video call; it targets people who meet face to face.

competitors.positioning: Free call recording and summaries built into phones.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Plaud is a separate device with better microphones and templates, but free built-in tools are its biggest long-term threat.

competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Plaud is more expensive but has more users, more retail reach and a more mature app.

guardrailMetrics: Privacy or data complaints and incidents
strengths: Rare hardware company with real recurring software revenue, over $100 million ARR
Grew mostly on its own sales, with very little outside funding
Strong retail and Amazon presence in many countries
Simple product: one button, clear outcome
Works for in-person meetings and phone calls, where software bots cannot go
weaknesses: Core AI is bought from model providers, so the software is easy to copy
Users pay twice (device and plan), which feels unfair to some
Depends on the phone app and cloud sync, which can fail
Light user data on long-term retention after the first year
risks: Apple, Google and Samsung building free recording and summaries into phones
Cheaper Chinese rivals and big players like ByteDance's Lark and Amazon's Bee
Recording consent laws vary by country and US state; misuse can create legal trouble
Data privacy concerns about where audio is stored and processed, especially for a company with roots in China
AI model price changes squeezing subscription margins
userComplaints: Free 300 minutes run out fast, and the subscription feels like a paywall after paying for hardware

Sync between device and app is sometimes slow or fails
Worries about privacy and cloud storage of sensitive conversations
Customer support is slow for returns and refunds

pmLessons: Hardware can be a customer acquisition channel for software. The device sale pays for the marketing, so the subscription is mostly profit.
Pick the moment where software alone fails. Plaud won in-person meetings and phone calls, which Zoom bots cannot reach.
A narrow, one-button product is easier to explain in a 30-second review, which helps retail and creator marketing.
When your core tech is bought from someone else, your edge must come from distribution, workflow and habit.

interviewQuestions.question: Plaud's free plan gives 300 minutes a month. How would you decide whether to raise or lower that limit?
interviewQuestions.hint: Explain the trade-off between activation and paid conversion. Look at the free-limit hit rate, upgrade rate after limit, retention and AI cost per minute. Propose an A/B test by region.

interviewQuestions.question: Apple adds free call recording and summaries to every iPhone. What should Plaud do?
interviewQuestions.hint: Separate where Apple wins (phone calls) from where Plaud wins (in-person rooms, better mics, job templates). Double down on professional workflows and integrations. Track churn among iPhone users.

interviewQuestions.question: What should Plaud's north star metric be?
interviewQuestions.hint: Pick something showing value delivered, like summaries opened or shared per week. Break it into active devices, recordings per user, summary usefulness and paid conversion.

interviewQuestions.question: Design a version of Plaud for doctors.
interviewQuestions.hint: Persona, pain (paperwork, accuracy, privacy), features (medical template, EHR export, local processing, consent prompts), pricing and success metric (minutes of paperwork saved).

interviewQuestions.question: Should Plaud make the device free and charge only a subscription?
interviewQuestions.hint: Compare upfront cash, return risk, churn, and how a free device changes who buys. Consider a bundle test at Costco. Watch payback period and renewal rate.
